title: Five Relationships and Mencius's Sprouts
bigQuestion: Are people born with the seeds of goodness, and what helps those seeds grow?

story.title: Three Houses
story.kicker: A mother moves house three times until her son copies the right neighbors.
paragraphs: An old Chinese story tells of a boy named Meng Ke and his mother. The boy's father had died, and his mother raised him alone. At first they lived near a graveyard.

Little Meng Ke watched the funerals. Soon he was playing funeral in the yard, pretending to dig graves and weep. His mother frowned. 'This is not the place for my son to grow up,' she said. So they moved.
Next they lived beside a busy market. The boy watched the sellers. Soon he was playing market, shouting prices and bargaining with pretend coins. His mother shook her head. They moved again.

This time they lived next to a school. The boy watched the students bow to their teacher. He watched them read and practice ceremonies. Soon he was bowing and reciting too. His mother smiled. 'This is the place,' she said. They stayed.
The boy grew up to be Mencius, one of the most famous teachers in Chinese history. People still tell this story about his mother. Many use it to talk about how much our surroundings shape us.
story.think: Why did the mother keep moving? How do the places around you shape what you do?

lessons.title: Five Pairs
lessons.mainIdea: Confucian teaching names five key relationships, each with its own duties.
reading: Confucian thinkers wrote about five key *relationships*. They are ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, older and younger sibling, and friend and friend.
The book Mencius lists them in 3A.4. It names a quality for each pair. Parent and child should share affection. Ruler and minister should share rightness. Friends should share trust.
The other two pairs have their own qualities in that list. Husband and wife each have their own roles. Older and younger should keep a proper order. Together, the five describe a whole society.

words.d: the way two people are connected, like parent and child or friends
ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, older and younger sibling, friend and friend

check.why: Parent and child is one of the five.

check.why: Friends should share trust or faithfulness.

lessons.title: Duties Both Ways
lessons.mainIdea: In Confucian teaching, each side of a relationship has duties, not only the lower one.
reading: People sometimes think the five relationships are only about obeying. But Confucian texts give duties to both sides. A parent must care for a child. A ruler must care for the people.
In Analects 12.11, a duke asked Confucius about good government. Confucius said: let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son.
Readers say this means each person should live up to their role. A ruler who is cruel is not being a true ruler. Mencius went further and said the people matter most in a state.

words.d: something a person should do because of their role
the part a person plays, like parent, friend or leader

look.title: Analects 12.11
look.text: Duke Jing of Qi asked about government. Confucius said: Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, and the son a son.
look.cite: Analects, book 12, passage 11, retold simply from James Legge's translation (1861)
look.prompt: What would it mean for a father to 'be a father' in this passage?

check.q: In Confucian teaching, who has duties in a relationship?
check.why: Both sides have duties, such as a parent caring for a child.

check.q: Who asked Confucius about government in Analects 12.11?
check.why: Duke Jing of Qi asked, and Confucius spoke of roles.

check.q: What does 'let the ruler be a ruler' mean, as readers explain it?
choices: Each person should live up to their role
check.why: Readers say each person should fulfill the duties of their role.

lessons.title: Hard Questions
lessons.mainIdea: People have debated the five relationships, especially the place of women, and they respond in many ways.
reading: Four of the five relationships put one person above the other. Only friends are equals. In old China, this often meant wives had less power than husbands. Daughters had fewer chances to study than sons.
Many people have questioned this. In the 1900s, Chinese writers and reformers criticized these rankings. They called for equal rights and schooling for girls and women.

Today readers respond in different ways. Some say the rankings belong to the past. Some keep the idea of care and duty but drop the ranking. Some scholars point to women who studied the classics long ago.

words.d: a person who works to change and improve a society
the same in value or rights

look.title: Two Responses
look.text: Reader A: The five relationships ranked people, and women were placed lower. That part should be left behind. Reader B: The idea that each role has duties of care is still useful, if everyone is treated as equal.
look.prompt: What does each reader keep, and what does each question?

check.q: How many of the five relationships put one person above the other?
check.why: Ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife and older-younger were ranked. Only friends were equals.

check.q: Who criticized these rankings in the 1900s?
check.why: Reformers in the 1900s called for equal rights for women.

check.q: What do some modern readers keep from the five relationships?
choices: The idea of care and duty, without the ranking
check.why: Some keep care and duty but drop the ranking.

lessons.title: The Second Sage
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius was a later Confucian teacher, often called the Second Sage, whose teachings fill a book of seven parts.
reading: *Mencius* is the Latin form of Mengzi, meaning Master Meng. He lived about a century after Confucius. Traditional dates are about 372 to 289 BCE, but these are not certain.
Mencius traveled from state to state. He talked with kings and tried to persuade them to rule with kindness. He also taught students who wrote down his talks.
The book Mencius has seven books, each in two parts, like 2A and 2B. Later Confucians called him the Second Sage, after Confucius. His book became one of the Four Books.

words.d: a Confucian teacher who lived about a century after Confucius; also the name of his book
a very wise person honored by a tradition

look.title: Two Teachers, Two Times

check.why: Mengzi means Master Meng; in English, Mencius.

check.q: What did later Confucians call Mencius?
check.why: He was honored as the Second Sage, after Confucius.

check.q: How is the book Mencius divided?
choices: Seven books, each in two parts
check.why: It has seven books, each split into A and B.

lessons.title: Mencius's Mother
lessons.mainIdea: A famous story says Mencius's mother moved three times to find a good place for her son to learn.
reading: The story of the three moves comes from an old book of stories about women, the Lienü zhuan. It was put together by Liu Xiang around the first century BCE, long after Mencius lived.

The same book tells a second story. Once young Mencius quit his studies early. His mother cut the cloth she was weaving. She said quitting learning was like ruining the cloth. He went back to study hard.
Historians cannot check these stories. But people in China have told them for over 2,000 years. They honor Mencius's mother as a model of a caring, wise parent.

words.d: the places and people around you
a person others look to as an example

look.title: Cutting the Cloth
look.text: Mencius came home early from his studies. His mother took a knife and cut the cloth on her loom. 'Quitting your learning,' she said, 'is like my cutting this cloth.' After that, Mencius studied day and night.
look.cite: Liu Xiang, Biographies of Exemplary Women (Lienü zhuan), book 1, story of the mother of Mencius, retold simply
look.prompt: Why do you think the mother chose to cut her cloth to teach this lesson?

check.q: Why did Mencius's mother move three times?
choices: To find a good place for him to learn
check.why: She wanted him near good examples, finally a school.

check.q: Where does the story of the moves come from?
check.why: It is told in Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women.

check.q: What did the mother cut to teach a lesson?
check.why: She cut her weaving to show what quitting does.

lessons.title: Talking With Kings
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius told kings to rule with humaneness and rightness rather than chasing profit.
reading: The book Mencius opens with a meeting. King Hui of Liang asks Mencius how he can profit the kingdom. It is found in Mencius 1A.1. It is one of the best-known scenes in the book.
Mencius answers: why must Your Majesty speak of profit? He says there is only humaneness and rightness. If everyone chases profit, from the king down, the kingdom will be in danger.
Mencius taught that a good ruler cares for the people like a parent. He said that if a ruler is cruel, the people may rightly turn away. This idea was bold in his time.

words.d: to try to get someone to agree or act by giving reasons
caring for other people; the English word for ren

look.title: Mencius 1A.1

look.cite: Mencius, book 1A, chapter 1, retold simply from James Legge's translation (The Works of Mencius, 1861)
look.prompt: Why might Mencius say chasing profit could put a kingdom in danger?

check.why: In 1A.1 the king asks about profit.

check.q: What did Mencius offer instead of profit?
check.why: Mencius says he has only humaneness and rightness to offer.

check.q: How did Mencius say a good ruler should treat the people?
check.why: He compared a good ruler to a caring parent.

lessons.title: The Child at the Well
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius argued that anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm and care at once.
reading: Mencius told a famous example in Mencius 2A.6. Imagine you suddenly see a small child about to fall into a well. What would you feel? He asked his listeners to picture it clearly.
Mencius said anyone would feel alarm and *compassion*. You would not feel it to win praise, or to please the child's parents. You would simply feel it, right away.
Mencius used this example to argue that people are born with a feeling of care for others. He said a person without it would hardly be human. This is his way of showing that human nature is good.

words.d: feeling for someone who is suffering and wanting to help
what people are like from birth

look.title: Mencius 2A.6
look.text: If people suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they all feel alarm and pity. Not to win friends with the parents, not to get praise, and not because they dislike the child's cry.
look.cite: Mencius, book 2A, chapter 6, retold simply from James Legge's translation (The Works of Mencius, 1861)
look.prompt: Why does Mencius list the reasons people do NOT feel alarm?

check.q: Where is the child at the well?
check.why: The child at the well is in Mencius 2A.6.

check.q: What did Mencius say anyone would feel?
check.why: He said everyone would feel alarm and pity at once.

check.q: What did Mencius use the example to argue?
choices: People are born with care for others
check.why: He argued human nature is good.

lessons.title: Four Sprouts
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius taught that four feelings in every person are sprouts that can grow into four virtues.
reading: In the same passage, Mencius named four *sprouts*. A sprout is a tiny new plant. He said every person is born with four feelings that are like sprouts.
The feeling of compassion is the sprout of ren. The feeling of shame at doing wrong is the sprout of yi. Modesty is the sprout of li. Knowing right from wrong is the sprout of wisdom.
Sprouts are small. Mencius taught they must be cared for to grow into full virtues. Like plants, they need the right conditions, just as his mother looked for the right home.

words.d: a tiny new plant; for Mencius, a small inborn feeling that can grow into a virtue
compassion, shame, modesty and knowing right from wrong, which Mencius said grow into four virtues
good judgment about what is true and right

look.title: Sprouts and Virtues

Knowing right from wrong grows into wisdom
look.cite: Mencius 2A.6, as translated by James Legge, The Works of Mencius (1861)
look.prompt: Which sprout grows into ren? Which grows into li?

check.q: What is a sprout, in Mencius's picture?
choices: A small inborn feeling that can grow
check.why: Sprouts are small feelings that can grow into virtues.

check.q: Which feeling is the sprout of ren?
check.why: Compassion is the sprout of ren.

check.q: What do sprouts need, as Mencius taught?
check.why: He taught that sprouts must be cared for to grow.

lessons.title: Ox Mountain and a Different View
lessons.mainIdea: Mencius said goodness can be damaged like a stripped mountain, while another Confucian, Xunzi, said goodness must be learned.
reading: In Mencius 6A.8, Mencius described Ox Mountain. Its trees were once beautiful. But people cut them down, and cattle ate every new shoot. Now it looks bare.
Mencius said people might think the mountain never had trees. But it did. In the same way, he said, a person who acts badly still had sprouts of goodness. They were just harmed.
Not all Confucians agreed. A later thinker, *Xunzi*, taught that human nature tends toward selfishness. He said goodness comes from learning and ritual. Readers still compare the two views.

words.d: a later Confucian thinker who taught that goodness must be learned through study and ritual
a bare hill in Mencius's story, used to show how goodness can be damaged

look.title: Two Confucian Views
look.text: Mencius: People are born with sprouts of goodness. With care, they grow. When harmed, they wither, like Ox Mountain. Xunzi: People are born tending toward selfishness. Teachers, study and ritual shape them into good people, as a craftsman straightens wood.
look.prompt: How are these two views alike? How are they different?

check.q: What happened to Ox Mountain in Mencius's story?
choices: Its trees were cut and its shoots eaten
check.why: In 6A.8, cutting and grazing left it bare.

check.q: What did Xunzi teach about human nature?
choices: It tends toward selfishness and needs shaping
check.why: Xunzi said goodness comes from learning and ritual.

check.q: Which thinker said people are born with sprouts of goodness?
check.why: Mencius taught the four sprouts.

review.q: Which pair is one of the five relationships?
review.why: Friend and friend is the one pair between equals.

Shame at wrong is the sprout of yi.

review.why: Reformers criticized ranking and called for equal rights for women.
